certainty_reasoning: The sexual/romantic characterization common in later biography was not reachable in the source so far (pointer to McKenna below), so the contested-single-source class with a disputed block is the honest mechanical proposal; a later check may raise it to consensus if two independent secondary attestations are verified.
date_label: Documented span Feb. 1892 (Wilde publicly calls the acquaintance 'extremely recent') through 1893 (Silverpoints published; The Blackmailers June 1893); the editors note Wilde and Gray later 'fell out' (undated). The conventional c. 1889 start rests on secondary tradition not read so far.
summary: Gray was publicly tied to Wilde by February 1892, when the Daily Telegraph called him Wilde's 'protege' - a label Wilde corrected in print while praising Gray's 'perfected mode of expression'. In June 1892 Wilde personally undertook the production costs of Gray's Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893), and after The Picture of Dorian Gray appeared, Gray 'referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so', though the editors find no evidence he was the character's original. The two fell out - the editors record the belief that Raffalovich broke the friendship up - but in De Profundis Wilde still ranked the friendship among those where 'my real life, my higher life' had been. Whether the bond was sexual rests on secondary claims not verified so far.

disputed.claim: That Wilde and Gray were lovers, conventionally dated c. 1889-93.
disputed.asserted_by: Later secondary tradition (e.g. McKenna 2003; commonly repeated in Wilde biography) - not verified in the source so far.
disputed.disputed_by: Wilde's own public statement (Daily Telegraph, printed 20 Feb. 1892) that the acquaintance was 'extremely recent'; Holland & Hart-Davis note there is 'no evidence for the persistent suggestion' that Gray was the original of Dorian Gray.
disputed.grounds: No first-person sexual attestation appears in the primary material read; the verified record documents patronage, the Dorian self-identification, retrospective affection in De Profundis, and a falling-out.

sources.quote: Your writer describes the author of the brilliant fantastic lecture on 'The Modern Actor' as 'a protégé' of mine. Allow me to state that my acquaintance with Mr John Gray is, I regret to say, extremely recent, and that I sought it because he had already a perfected mode of expression both in prose and verse. … These qualities Mr John Gray possesses in a marked degree. He needs no other protection, nor, indeed, would he accept it.
sources.context: Wilde to the Editor of the Daily Telegraph, 19 February [1892], published 20 February headed puppets and actors; 'a protégé' italicised in original
sources.supports: The public 'protege' characterization and Wilde's printed denial of it ('extremely recent'), Feb. 1892
sources.provenance: PDF page 540, printed folio 520 confirmed on rendered page. Elision drops four sentences on artists needing protection; full text in long-form notes.

sources.quote: Dear Sir, Silverpoints (poems) by John Gray. We agree to issue the above book in the autumn on your undertaking the cost of the designs – block for same – paper, printing and binding of an edition not exceeding 250 copies.
sources.context: Mathews and Lane (The Bodley Head) to Wilde, 17 June 1892, Vigo Street - the publishers' agreement printed in Complete Letters; Silverpoints italicised in original ! Corrected : this carried no speaker, so the page fell back to the volume's author and printed the publishers' letter as Wilde writing - and once the addressee was recorded, as Wilde writing to himself.
sources.supports: Wilde personally undertook the production costs of Gray's Silverpoints - the patronage in a primary document
sources.provenance: PDF page 547, printed folio 527 confirmed on rendered page.
sources.speaker: Elkin Mathews and John Lane (The Bodley Head)

sources.quote: His book of poems, Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893), was designed by Ricketts, and initially underwritten by Wilde … before they fell out. … While there is no evidence for the persistent suggestion that he was the original of Dorian Gray, after the publication of the story he referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote on John Gray
sources.supports: The falling-out; the 'Dorian' self-identification with the editors' no-evidence caveat
sources.provenance: PDF page 540, printed folio 520 confirmed on rendered page. First elision drops the cross-reference '(see p.527)'; second bridges two non-adjacent footnote sentences; full footnote content in long-form notes.

sources.quote: When I compare my friendship with you to my friendship with such still younger men as John Gray and Pierre Louÿs I feel ashamed. My real life, my higher life was with them and such as they.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas ('De Profundis'), HM Prison, Reading, January-March 1897
sources.supports: Wilde's retrospective valuation of the Gray friendship - 'my real life, my higher life'
sources.provenance: PDF page 737, printed folio 686 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: In fact, the John Gray that Oscar met and fell in love with was a construction, an exquisite fiction, a carefully crafted sonnet of a young man, hewn and marvellously fashioned from very rough clay.
sources.context: McKenna opening his account of Gray's origins - born in Bethnal Green, son of a Woolwich Dockyard wheelwright, set to work at thirteen as an apprentice metal-turner. At PDF p. 239 McKenna adds that Gray was 'still Oscar's officially beloved'. Both are assertions, unlike the page at PDF 216, where he only poses the question whether Wilde led Gray or Gray led Wilde.
sources.supports: The sexual-relationship characterization underlying the 'alleged' claim; requires verification in the source
sources.provenance: PDF page 194. Re-pointed from the mckenna-2003 pointer to the 2008 edition held; no printed folios, so the locator is PDF page. This replaces the earlier candidate at PDF 216, which was interrogative and could not carry the claim.
